title: The Limits of AI as an Economic Weapon
gist: Bessler argues AI is splitting into a pharma-like divided market where cheap Chinese open-weight models take most token volume (e.g. 56% of Vercel gateway tokens but 14% of spend) while closed U.S. frontier models keep a smaller premium tier. Because good-enough substitutes are free, AI models cannot be a U.S. coercive chokepoint, echoing Japan's DRAM dominance in the 1980s. The real U.S. levers are Nvidia-dominated compute and American cloud hosting, so Washington should keep chip controls narrow and keep the clouds American.

themes.theme: Divided AI market: commodity open-weight vs premium closed models

insights.claim: Global AI demand is likely to fragment into a 'divided market': a large commoditized pool of cheap or free open-weight models and a smaller premium tier of closed frontier models.
insights.speaker: Max Bessler
insights.so_what: Expect margin compression on routine AI workloads; frontier-lab pricing power concentrates in a shrinking slice of complex tasks.
insights.quote: global demand for AI products will likely fragment into a “divided market” split between a larger commoditized pool and a smaller premium echelon of offerings
insights.locator: Today, any user with access to

insights.claim: Routine AI tasks such as simple advice, web research, and writing are still often sent to expensive models but will become table stakes for any off-the-shelf model, leaving premium models to dominate a smaller set of complex, as-yet-unknown applications.
insights.speaker: Max Bessler
insights.so_what: Revenue tied to commodity tasks (chat, search, writing) is at risk of being repriced toward zero.
insights.locator: Today, any user with access to

insights.claim: The pharmaceutical market is the template for AI's split: generics account for 90% of U.S. prescriptions but only 12% of spending, while branded drugs are 10% of prescriptions but 88% of spending.
insights.speaker: Max Bessler
insights.so_what: Model AI vendor economics like pharma: the volume tier is commoditized, profits accrue to the differentiated premium tier.
insights.quote: 90% of all prescriptions are generic drugs but make up only 12% of spending; brands capture only 10% of prescriptions but take home 88% of all spending
insights.locator: Such divided markets exist elsewhere today.

insights.claim: Buyers pay a premium for AI only when the capability gap is worth it; below that threshold they choose on cost, so open models need only be 'good enough' rather than match the frontier.
insights.speaker: Max Bessler
insights.so_what: Frontier benchmark leads do not protect market share in the cost-sensitive majority of usage.
insights.quote: Are these open models as capable as closed models? No, but they’re good enough.
insights.locator: Are these open models as capable

insights.claim: Benchmarks such as Epoch and METR indicate the best Chinese open models still trail the American frontier, but that lag does not prevent them from taking the commoditized tier.
insights.speaker: Max Bessler
insights.so_what: Chinese capability lag is not a reliable moat for U.S. labs' volume business.
insights.locator: Are these open models as capable

insights.claim: Sophisticated companies already split usage: cheap open-weight models for routine tasks and selective payment for closed models like Claude for harder jobs.
insights.speaker: Max Bessler
insights.so_what: Multi-model routing is becoming standard enterprise practice, pressuring blended revenue per token for closed labs.
insights.quote: Companies that use cheap open-weight models for routine tasks can still selectively pay for Claude when needed for tougher jobs.
insights.locator: Are these open models as capable

themes.theme: Usage data on Chinese open-weight adoption

insights.claim: Vercel's September 2026 gateway report found open-weight models processed 56% of August's gateway tokens but accounted for only 14% of spend, mirroring the generic-drug split.
insights.speaker: Max Bessler
insights.so_what: Hard evidence the volume/value split is already occurring; token share and revenue share are diverging.
insights.quote: “Open-weight models processed 56% of August’s gateway tokens and accounted for 14% of spend.”
insights.locator: Motivated businesses and savvy consumers

insights.claim: According to a July CNBC report, the share of tokens used by U.S. companies on Chinese models via OpenRouter has stayed above 30% since February and peaked as high as 46%.
insights.speaker: Max Bessler
insights.so_what: Chinese models have substantial penetration even among U.S. corporate users, despite political headwinds.
insights.locator: Motivated businesses and savvy consumers

insights.claim: Hugging Face found that most of its 2025 trending models were developed in China or derived from a Chinese-developed model.
insights.speaker: Max Bessler
insights.so_what: China dominates the open-weight developer ecosystem and its mindshare.
insights.quote: “either developed in China or derivative of a model developed in China.”
insights.locator: Motivated businesses and savvy consumers

insights.claim: Industry-wide AI usage figures are unreliable: OpenAI's API alone reportedly moves about six and a half times as many tokens per month as every model on OpenRouter combined, so gateway data may overstate open-model share.
insights.speaker: Max Bessler
insights.so_what: Treat gateway-based open-model share stats with caution; they are a skewed sample of total usage.
insights.quote: “OpenAI’s API alone moves roughly six and a half times as many tokens each month as every model on OpenRouter combined”
insights.locator: Measuring AI usage is inherently difficult

insights.claim: Firms have incentives to hide their use of Chinese open models, both because disclosing AI usage can reveal corporate strategy and because admitting reliance on Beijing-controlled models carries political costs in the U.S.
insights.speaker: Max Bessler
insights.so_what: Actual Chinese-model adoption is likely under-reported, so the market shift may be larger than visible.
insights.locator: Measuring AI usage is inherently difficult

themes.theme: Frontier lab economics and the military-funding argument

insights.claim: Daniel Francis argues the flood of Chinese open models is an 'economic attack on U.S. military development' because a growing commoditized layer starves frontier labs of the profits they need to build the best models for the military.
insights.speaker: Daniel Francis
insights.so_what: Frontier-lab profitability is framed as a national-security issue, raising odds of government support or intervention.
insights.locator: The stakes are high for a market

insights.claim: Francis proposes a federal subsidy for frontier labs to reserve their most advanced models for government use, which would also prevent distillation, while releasing only 'heavily neutered' models to the public and keeping open-weight models out.
insights.speaker: Daniel Francis
insights.so_what: A policy path exists in which frontier labs become quasi-defense contractors with government-backed revenue.
insights.locator: To overcome this erosion of the frontier

insights.claim: The author counters that a model reserved for government never diffuses and therefore creates no chokepoint, so Francis's plan preserves AI for military and cyberwarfare use while forfeiting peaceful economic coercion.
insights.speaker: Max Bessler
insights.so_what: Subsidy-and-withhold policy would protect defense capabilities but not the global commercial reach of U.S. labs.
insights.quote: A model that never diffuses is no chokepoint, and leaves no lever for Washington to pull.
insights.locator: To overcome this erosion of the frontier

insights.claim: U.S. frontier labs are profit-driven and have little incentive to build top-tier open-weight models, so China is likely to dominate the open-weight sector for the foreseeable future.
insights.speaker: Max Bessler
insights.so_what: Do not expect U.S. labs to contest the commodity tier; Chinese open-weight share likely persists.
insights.quote: it seems likely that for the foreseeable future China will dominate the open-weight sector
insights.locator: In Silicon Valley, labs are locked

themes.theme: Weaponized interdependence and the AI chokepoint test

insights.claim: Since WWII Washington has used the global footprint of U.S. tech firms as a coercion tool, e.g. cutting Huawei off from Google's Android in 2019 and TSMC chips in 2020, after which Huawei's global smartphone share fell from 20% in 2020 to virtually nothing outside mainland China by 2024.
insights.speaker: Max Bessler
insights.so_what: Precedent shows U.S. tech chokepoints can destroy a foreign champion's international business when substitutes are absent.
insights.locator: When technology firms go abroad

insights.claim: Henry Farrell and Abraham Newman's 'weaponized interdependence' describes how firms chasing profit inadvertently give states levers to extend influence across borders.
insights.speaker: Max Bessler
insights.so_what: Useful lens for assessing which tech positions carry geopolitical (and sanctions) risk or leverage.
insights.locator: When technology firms go abroad

insights.claim: Cisco illustrates the pattern: in fiscal 1998 it sold $8.5 billion of equipment that cost $2.9 billion to make, and its routers carried so much internet traffic that the NSA reportedly planted 'beacons' in Cisco gear.
insights.speaker: Max Bessler
insights.so_what: Dominant infrastructure vendors become intelligence and policy nodes, which shapes foreign buyers' trust and substitution behavior.
insights.quote: In fiscal year 1998, Cisco sold $8.5 billion of equipment that cost it $2.9 billion to make.
insights.locator: In the late 20th century, Cisco

insights.claim: Edward Fishman defines an economic chokepoint by three conditions: dominant concentrated market share held by one country or close allies, no short-term substitutes, and the ability to impose asymmetric pain with minimal self-harm.
insights.speaker: Edward Fishman
insights.so_what: A checklist for judging which parts of the AI stack carry pricing power and geopolitical leverage.
insights.locator: For this strategy to be successful

insights.claim: AI models fail Fishman's chokepoint test because free, downloadable, improving Chinese open-weight substitutes spread usage across models Washington cannot control, so AI models cannot serve as an effective U.S. economic weapon.
insights.speaker: Max Bessler
insights.so_what: The model layer is unlikely to command monopoly-like rents or strategic premium.
insights.quote: a divided AI market denies Washington the use of AI as a chokepoint, crippling its viability as an economic weapon for U.S. policymakers
insights.locator: Yet, a divided AI market denies

insights.claim: Trying to weaponize AI models by sanctioning Chinese ones could backfire, spurring more open-source development in China, Europe, or the U.S. and pushing allies toward sovereign models likely built on Chinese open weights.
insights.speaker: Max Bessler
insights.so_what: Restrictions on Chinese models would likely accelerate open-weight proliferation and sovereign-AI spending rather than help U.S. labs.
insights.quote: “every time Washington weaponizes a chokepoint, other countries take steps to insulate themselves from it”
insights.locator: Yet, a divided AI market denies

insights.claim: Putting companies that use Chinese models on an entity list would needlessly disrupt U.S. firms and weaken their influence, since Washington cannot restrict open-source models without upsetting cost-conscious users at home and abroad.
insights.speaker: Max Bessler
insights.so_what: Broad bans on Chinese open models look politically and economically costly, lowering their probability.
insights.locator: Today, both Washington and Silicon Valley

themes.theme: Winners of the divided market and industry politics

insights.claim: Nvidia benefits from a divided AI market because cheap Chinese open-weight models drive demand for domestic data centers that run them.
insights.speaker: Max Bessler
insights.so_what: Open-weight proliferation is bullish for compute demand regardless of which lab wins.
insights.quote: a boon for Nvidia, which benefits directly from the demand for domestic data centers running Chinese models
insights.locator: Other American firms—that aren’t frontier labs

insights.claim: U.S. corporations, especially startups, benefit because cheap open-weight models let them automate tasks too expensive to run on Claude or GPT.
insights.speaker: Max Bessler
insights.so_what: Lower inference costs expand the addressable market for AI-enabled applications and startups.
insights.locator: Other American firms—that aren’t frontier labs

insights.claim: In July, after Anthropic accused Chinese labs of distilling Claude and releasing the results as open weights, Nvidia led more than 270 tech companies in an open letter against restrictions on Chinese open-weight models; OpenAI and Google signed late and Anthropic has not signed.
insights.speaker: Max Bessler
insights.so_what: Industry lobbying is aligned against open-weight restrictions, signaling low odds of such policy and a split between Nvidia and frontier labs.
insights.locator: Other American firms—that aren’t frontier labs

themes.theme: DRAM precedent: losing the commodity layer, winning one layer up

insights.claim: Japan captured the commoditized DRAM market in the 1980s without out-innovating Silicon Valley; by 1987 NEC, Toshiba, and Hitachi had pushed Japan's global DRAM share to 80 percent.
insights.speaker: Max Bessler
insights.so_what: Historical analogue suggests China's open-weight dominance may resemble a commodity win with thin margins.
insights.quote: By 1987, chipmakers NEC, Toshiba, and Hitachi had pushed Japan’s share of the global DRAM market to 80 percent.
insights.locator: This story has played out before.

insights.claim: The U.S. responded with SEMATECH and a MITI-negotiated agreement targeting slightly above 20 percent foreign share of Japan's DRAM market, and American firms regained half the world semiconductor market by the mid-1990s.
insights.speaker: Max Bessler
insights.so_what: Industrial policy can help, but the durable recovery came from strategic repositioning.
insights.locator: In response, Washington engaged in a series

insights.claim: What actually saved Bay Area chipmakers was exiting DRAM and moving up the value chain into PCs, microprocessors, workstations, and networking built on commoditized memory; profits stayed in California while Japan gained little.
insights.speaker: Max Bessler
insights.so_what: In AI, value may accrue to firms building applications on commodity models rather than to commodity model makers.
insights.quote: What ultimately saved Bay Area firms in the 1990s was leaving the DRAM market and moving up the value chain into more profitable offerings.
insights.locator: Did America win again?

insights.claim: Even with 80 percent of the DRAM market Japan could not coerce anyone, because a commodity with many manufacturers and easy substitutes offers nothing to withhold; the same will be true for whoever dominates commoditized AI models.
insights.speaker: Max Bessler
insights.so_what: China's open-weight lead is unlikely to give Beijing coercive leverage or pricing power either.
insights.quote: Washington would not be able to win it as a lever, but neither would anyone else.
insights.locator: DRAM, while an economic success

insights.claim: If AI divides like DRAM, application companies such as Harvey and Thomson Reuters will be paid directly by customers while Moonshot and Alibaba struggle to profit even as their models do the work.
insights.speaker: Max Bessler
insights.so_what: Favors application-layer businesses over commodity model providers on margin capture.
insights.quote: customers of Harvey and Thomson Reuters pay the companies directly, while Moonshot and Alibaba struggle to profit even as their models do all the work

themes.theme: Where real U.S. chokepoints remain: compute and cloud

insights.claim: Compute passes the chokepoint test: 39.7 million petaflops of AI compute sit in the United States versus 400,000 in China, and Nvidia holds more than 85 percent of the AI chip market.
insights.speaker: Max Bessler
insights.so_what: Chip export controls remain the strongest U.S. lever, sustaining Nvidia's strategic and market position.
insights.quote: 39.7 million petaflops of AI compute live in the United States, compared to just 400,000 in China
insights.locator: Even in a divided AI market

insights.claim: Chip export controls slow Chinese labs but are not enough to knock China out of the race, as the continued success of Chinese open-weight models shows.
insights.speaker: Max Bessler
insights.so_what: Do not assume export controls will halt Chinese model competitiveness.
insights.locator: Even in a divided AI market

insights.claim: The binding domestic constraint on building the best models is not Nvidia chip supply but how fast the U.S. can power and permit data centers.
insights.speaker: Max Bessler
insights.so_what: Power generation and data-center permitting are key bottlenecks and beneficiaries of AI capex.
insights.quote: the constraint on developing the best models is not how many chips Nvidia can sell, but how fast the country can power and permit the data centers to run them
insights.locator: Export controls work on chips

insights.claim: Selling too few chips to China risks spurring indigenization and hurting Nvidia's profits, but selling too many is the greater risk because it accelerates China's ability to match U.S. frontier labs.
insights.speaker: Max Bessler
insights.so_what: Export-control policy will keep oscillating on a narrow band, a persistent source of Nvidia China-revenue uncertainty.
insights.locator: Export controls work on chips

insights.claim: AI hosting and inference is a second chokepoint: U.S. clouds hold over 70 percent of the market, Moonshot is negotiating to place Kimi K3 on all three largest clouds, and Thomson Reuters and Harvey already build on Qwen and Kimi K3.
insights.speaker: Max Bessler
insights.so_what: U.S. hyperscalers stand to capture value from Chinese open models by hosting them.
insights.quote: U.S. clouds hold over 70 percent of the market
insights.locator: Export controls work on chips

insights.claim: Washington should keep chip controls narrow and keep clouds American so the U.S. hosts the world's cheap models; it may not dictate which model people use but can own where models run.
insights.speaker: Max Bessler
insights.so_what: Policy direction favors U.S. cloud providers and chip vendors over frontier model labs as strategic assets.
insights.quote: Maybe the U.S. can no longer tell you what model to use, but it can own where that model runs.
insights.locator: The future of the world AI industry
